input_signals.name: Value Gated by Going-Concern Flags
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(re, 0), INDICATOR(SUB(act, lct), 0)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The value premium is conditional: it accrues to cheap firms with positive retained earnings and positive working capital, while cheap firms failing both going-concern screens have valuations that reflect genuine default risk and earn no premium.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator sum acts as a 0/1/2 multiplier that switches the value exposure off for firms with a deficit in accumulated earnings and a liquidity shortfall, so extreme cheapness among distressed firms is collapsed to the bottom of the cross-section. This is an explicitly conditional interaction rather than an additive blend of two effects. Winsorizing book-to-market prevents a handful of near-zero-market-cap firms from dominating the long leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ), add( indicator( re, 0 ), indicator( sub( act, lct ), 0 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Weakest-Link Value Solvency Score
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Compensated value requires cheapness and solvency jointly, so the firm's score should be its worst dimension: a deeply cheap firm with no accumulated earnings and no cash relative to debt is a distress trap, not a value opportunity, and must not be rescued by its cheapness rank.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the additive SUMRANK blend with MIN of the two ranked dimensions makes the score non-compensatory, so a firm ranks high only if it is simultaneously in the cheap tail and the solvent tail — the claim the earlier version could not support. Both arguments are rescaled to a common [0,1] rank metric before the MIN so neither dimension mechanically dominates the binding constraint. The short leg is now firms that are weak on at least one dimension, which is precisely the expensive-or-distressed population the economic story targets.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( re, at ), ratio( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Working-Capital Backed Cheapness
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: If the liquidation-backing effect is about near-term funding safety rather than full solvency, then netting only current liabilities from current assets should capture most of it; if long-term creditor claims are what separate healthy from distressed cheapness, this variant should be markedly weaker.
input_signals.reasoning: This is deliberately a one-input contrast with the archive winner: it removes long-term liabilities from the netting so that the difference in results identifies whether the alpha comes from short-horizon liquidity or from total creditor overhang. That distinction matters economically because the two imply different risks — refinancing pressure versus permanent capital impairment — and it cannot be inferred from the existing evaluations. Winsorization matches the archive construction so the comparison is not confounded by scaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( act, lct ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Liquidation Backing With Cash Generation
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lct)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net liquid asset backing is a stock of safety that a cash-burning firm consumes; cheapness is genuinely healthy only when the liquid cushion is not being eroded by operating outflows relative to current obligations.
input_signals.reasoning: The MIN structure makes the score high only when both the liquidation cushion and the operating cash coverage of current liabilities are strong, so it tests whether adding a flow condition to the winning stock condition sharpens the FF5 alpha or merely shrinks the eligible universe. Because a static balance-sheet cushion says nothing about its rate of depletion, this is the most economically natural refinement of the archive's best result rather than a rescaling of it. If the alpha rises with only mild coverage loss, the mechanism is confirmed as solvency plus sustainability; if not, the effect is purely a stock-of-liquidity phenomenon.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: Absolute Liquidation Discount to Firm Size
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), at), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The compensated form of cheapness is an absolute dollar discount of market capitalization below net liquid asset value, sized relative to the firm's asset base rather than relative to its own depressed price, so that the signal measures the margin of safety rather than the smallness of the price.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not a monotone transform of the archived winner: the discount enters as a difference rather than a quotient and is deflated by total assets instead of market capitalization, so the quantile portfolios and their size composition genuinely change. That distinction is the substantive test the critic asked for — if the archived alpha is really a micro-cap price-scaling artifact it should weaken here, whereas if it is a true asset-value discount it should survive with a better behaved regressor and a stronger FMB slope. Winsorization handles the residual tail without altering the ordering of the bulk of firms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), at ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Cheapness Backed by Liquid Book Quality
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ceq)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Two firms with the same book-to-market differ in whether their book equity is composed of liquid assets net of all claims or of fixed and intangible assets standing behind creditors; only cheapness whose book value is liquid-backed is compensated, because that collateral survives a downturn.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a dollar complement collapses to non-current-assets-to-price, a known positively priced quantity with the wrong sign, so the revision changes the construct to a *composition* ratio — net liquid assets as a fraction of book equity — which is a quality-of-book measure, not an assets-to-price measure. The MIN form makes the score high only when the firm is both cheap and liquid-backed, so it directly separates the two kinds of cheap firms the theme is about rather than re-testing the value premium. It also asks a question the archive cannot answer: whether the liquidation effect works through book quality conditional on cheapness or only through the absolute price discount.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), ceq ) ) )

input_signals.name: Revenue Cheapness With Solvent Liquidity
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The healthy-cheap versus trap distinction should not be specific to balance-sheet valuation: a firm cheap on revenue is a compensated value case when its current assets already exceed all liabilities, and a distressed one when creditors have first claim on the entire asset base.
input_signals.reasoning: Every liquidation-family result in the archive uses a balance-sheet numerator over price, so the effect could be a mechanical book-to-market artifact; substituting a revenue-based valuation anchor tests whether liquid solvency conditions the value premium generally or only its book-based form. Deflating the cushion by assets here is deliberate — the price dimension already enters through the sales multiple, so the two legs stay economically independent. Sales are reported nearly universally, so coverage should match the archive's best signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( revt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cushion Discount Without Dilution
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Management's financing behavior reveals which kind of cheap firm it is running: a firm sitting on a liquid cushion that keeps issuing shares is funding losses and diluting the very claim that looks cheap, whereas one whose share count is flat or shrinking is letting existing holders keep the discount.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces a neutralization transform with a genuinely new arbiter — the corporate financing decision — which is observable, forward-looking, and absent from every archive signal that has relied purely on balance-sheet stocks and accounting flows. Share count changes are reported for essentially all firms, so unlike the operating-cash-flow filter this conditioning costs almost no coverage, and it should sharpen the deep-discount decile by removing serial issuers whose cushion per share is eroding. It also gives the batch a direct test of whether the cushion alpha is an ownership-dilution phenomenon rather than an asset-value phenomenon.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( growth( csho, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Two-Sided Cushion and Earnings Stability Score
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The theme has two distinct payoffs — asset-backed cheapness earns a premium and option-like unstable-earnings equity loses — so a score that is high for over-collateralized firms with stable fundamentals and low for liability-heavy firms with volatile fundamentals should capture both sides in one spread.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive documents the long side (cushion discount, +6%) and the short side (volatile-earnings stub, −4.4% with t=−3.27) as separate signals; rank-averaging them keeps the deep-discount firms at the top rather than filtering them out, while the volatility leg populates the bottom with genuine lottery-like stubs instead of merely levered firms. Because SUMRANK is additive, the middle of the distribution becomes monotone in two economically independent channels, which is the structural fix for the near-zero FMB slopes that pure tail signals produce. The five-year volatility window costs modest coverage, as the stub signal's 0.130 shows.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( vol( ratio( pi, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Productive Cushion at a Discount
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms trading below net liquid asset value split into two economically opposite groups — working businesses whose inventory and receivables are turning over to generate sales, and dormant shells whose current assets sit idle while overhead consumes them — and only the productive group's discount closes.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces asset productivity, a channel the archive has never tested, in place of recombining two collinear cushion constructs: revenue per dollar of current assets says whether the collateral is a live operating base or a stagnant pile, which is the sharpest available distinction between compensated cheapness and a slow-burning trap. Because the second leg shares the current-asset base with the first, it should refine the deep-discount decile rather than displace it — the failure mode the no-dilution intersection exposed. Both inputs are universally reported, so coverage should hold near the archive's 0.12.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( revt, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap Book Value in Asset-Heavy Firms
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), revt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the effect is really about balance-sheet dominance rather than about the specific net-net threshold, then ordinary book-to-market conditioned on a large liquid cushion per dollar of revenue should reproduce it; if instead the price-below-liquid-assets condition is essential, this variant will be much weaker.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive ablation the archive still lacks: every strong result has used net liquid assets in the numerator over price, so we cannot yet tell whether the alpha requires that specific comparison or only requires cheapness plus an operations-light liquid balance sheet. Book-to-market has repeatedly produced strong FMB slopes (3.5–4.0) with weak or negative alphas in this archive, so pairing it with the newly identified conditioner tests directly whether that conditioner is what converts a factor-explained value tilt into abnormal return. Coverage matches the archive's best signals since all inputs are standard.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), revt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Discount With Uninflated Working Capital
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(SUB(GROWTH(act, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A liquid cushion is only worth its carrying value if it is turning over; when current assets grow far faster than sales, the balance sheet is accumulating unsellable inventory and uncollectible receivables, so the apparent liquidation floor is overstated and the cheapness is a genuine distress signal.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive test of cushion quality has varied which claims are netted or how large the cushion is; none has questioned whether the reported current assets are realizable, which is exactly the accounting failure that turns a net-net into a trap. The leg is a difference of two growth rates, so it is continuously distributed and roughly symmetric — the property that lifted the FMB slope in the two-sided score — while remaining economically tied to the cushion rather than orthogonal to it. This is the batch's most direct attempt to raise the cross-sectional slope without truncating the alpha-bearing tail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( sub( growth( act, 1 ), growth( revt, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt-Free Cash Earnings Yield
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), act))))
input_signals.hypothesis: On the earnings side of valuation, cheapness is compensated when no enforceable debt stands between the operating cash flow and the shareholder; a high cash-earnings yield with interest-bearing debt small relative to liquid assets is the going-concern analogue of a net-net.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has tested the earnings channel almost exclusively on the trap side — high yield with high leverage or high fixed charges, both around −4% alpha — so the symmetric positive case has never been evaluated, leaving the theme's central claim only half tested. Scaling debt by current assets rather than total assets measures whether the enforceable claims could be extinguished immediately, which is the distress-relevant comparison and mirrors the construct that scored best in generation 5 (5.6% alpha, t=4.11). Both legs are broadly reported, so coverage should stay near 0.14.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), act ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Discount With Non-Expanding Claims
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(lt, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A liquid cushion priced at a discount is safe only if creditors are not expanding their claim on it; rising total liabilities mean the firm is funding operations by borrowing against the very assets that constitute the margin of safety.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has conditioned the cushion on its own change and on share issuance but never on the growth of the claims that are netted out of it, even though liability expansion is the mechanism by which a net-net silently becomes a levered shell. The leg is cushion-related through lt, so it should refine rather than displace the top decile — the distinction generation 4 established between correlated and orthogonal conditioners. It also gives a clean contrast with Signal 3: asset-side inflation versus liability-side expansion as competing explanations for why a cushion fails to protect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( growth( lt, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Negative Implied Price of Operations
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(act, lt)), revt)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Market capitalization decomposes into the net liquid cushion plus whatever the market is paying for the operating business; when that residual stub price is deeply negative relative to the revenue the business actually produces, investors are being handed the operations for free because they extrapolate current operating disappointment.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than re-scaling the cushion by another operating denominator — the collinearity the critic identified — this construct isolates the *residual* the archive has never measured: price minus cushion, which is the market's standalone valuation of the going concern, benchmarked against the revenue that concern generates. It states the theme's core question directly, because a negative stub price means the valuation reflects operating distress while the distress-relevant collateral is intact and unpriced. Revenue is strictly positive for the operating universe, so the deflator does not sign-flip, and the measure is continuous across the whole cross-section rather than being a tail indicator.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( neg( ratio( sub( mul( prcc_f, csho ), sub( act, lt ) ), revt ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Claims Value per Dollar of Liquid Assets
input_signals.expression: NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Every claim on a firm — equity at market value and liabilities at face value — is ultimately a claim on its assets, so the price the market places on each dollar of liquid current assets is the cleanest statement of asset-backed cheapness; paying little for each such dollar is compensated, paying much is not.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not a monotone transform of the total-claims cushion signal: that measure is (act−lt)/(ME+lt), a function of two independent ratios, whereas this is (ME+lt)/act, which orders firms differently whenever leverage and market valuation move apart. Because the denominator is gross current assets, the quantity is strictly positive and bounded away from the explosive skew that has kept the archive's FMB slopes near zero, giving a plausible path to joint strength rather than tail-only alpha. It also treats creditors and shareholders symmetrically, which is the correct economics when asking what the market pays for liquid collateral.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: neg( winsor( ratio( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), lt ), act ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap Liquid Assets With Covered Claims
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)), RATIO(pi, lt))
input_signals.hypothesis: Healthy cheapness combines a low price per dollar of liquid assets with pretax earnings large enough to service the outstanding claims; the trap is the opposite corner, where claims are expensive relative to liquid assets and earnings cannot cover them.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not an operator swap on an existing pair: both legs are new to the archive — the price paid per dollar of liquid assets and pretax income scaled by total claims rather than by assets, which measures debt-service capacity rather than profitability. Because the two legs use different accounting anchors and neither is a monotone function of the other, the additive score populates its extremes with economically different firms, giving genuinely new portfolio evidence rather than a smoothed version of a tested spread. Both components are continuously distributed across essentially the whole universe, which is the property most likely to convert the archive's tail-only alpha into a signal with a coherent cross-sectional slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( neg( ratio( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), lt ), act ) ), ratio( pi, lt ) )

input_signals.name: Cushion Depth Plus Cheap Liquid Assets
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The depth of the net-of-claims discount and the price paid per gross dollar of liquid assets are two distinct statements about the same balance sheet — the first is extreme and tail-concentrated, the second smooth and pervasive — and a firm ranked highly on both is cheap in a way that neither measure alone establishes.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the last disciplined attempt to close the archive's central gap: the first leg carries essentially all of the documented alpha (5.9%, t=4.48) but a slope of 0.48, while the second leg carries a 4.17 slope and Sharpe 0.411 with almost no alpha, and the two are related but not monotone transforms of one another since one nets liabilities out of the numerator and the other adds them to it. Additive combination keeps deeply discounted firms near the top instead of intersecting them away, so a mid-to-high single-digit alpha with a slope above 2 is a realistic outcome rather than a smoothing artifact. If it succeeds it becomes the final recommended signal; if it fails, the evidence will have shown the alpha and the slope to be genuinely irreconcilable in this family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( ratio( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), lt ), act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cushion Depth Plus Claim Coverage by Earnings
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(pi, lt))
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset-backed cheapness and the ability to service outstanding claims out of current earnings are the two independent guarantees a cheap equity can offer; the firms that provide both are the compensated value cases, and those providing neither are the distressed traps whose price is a forecast.
input_signals.reasoning: Pretax income scaled by total liabilities is a debt-service capacity measure rather than a profitability measure, and it appeared in the archive only alongside the alpha-free claims-per-liquid-asset leg, so its pairing with the alpha-carrying discount has never been observed. The leg is smooth and roughly symmetric across the cross-section, the property that converted the generation-8 composite into the archive's only jointly strong signal, while remaining a distress variable rather than a second valuation ratio. Comparing its outcome with Signal 1 identifies whether the missing slope is best supplied by a second valuation anchor or by a solvency-flow channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), ratio( pi, lt ) )

input_signals.name: Free Liquid Assets After Claims and Price
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), act), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: For each dollar of liquid assets a firm holds, some part is owed to creditors, some part is already paid for by the equity market, and the remainder is free value handed to the buyer; the size of that free remainder per dollar of liquid assets is the cleanest single statement of collateral-backed mispricing.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the weighted kitchen-sink rank blend with one interpretable ratio that is not a monotone transform of any archive signal: deflating the dollar discount by total assets destroyed the alpha (−1.9%) while deflating by market value produced the tail-only champion, and gross current assets is the intermediate deflator that keeps the market price inside the numerator where it belongs while bounding the measure from above. Because the denominator is a positive, slowly varying scale variable, the resulting regressor is smooth across the whole cross-section rather than concentrated in a skewed tail, which is exactly the property associated with usable Fama-MacBeth slopes in this archive. It combines the discount, the claims, and the price in a single economic quantity rather than averaging three ranked proxies with implicit unequal weights.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), act ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Expensive Collateral With Eroding Earned Capital
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The genuine trap is not a cheap levered firm but one where all claims — market equity plus creditor claims — are priced expensively against the liquid assets backing them while accumulated earned capital erodes year after year, so the claim structure is overvalued relative to shrinking substance.
input_signals.reasoning: The valuation leg is deliberately oriented toward expensiveness rather than leverage, which repairs the sign inconsistency the critic identified: the archive shows the negated form of this exact ratio produced an FMB slope of +4.17, so the un-negated form should deliver a reliably negative slope aligned with the negative expected sign, unlike every liabilities-to-market-value construction tried so far. Pairing it additively with the multi-year erosion of earned capital keeps both legs smooth and continuous, so the bottom of the score is a differentiated population rather than the undifferentiated mixture that MIN gates produced on the short side. This is the archive's best remaining chance at a short-side signal with both metrics pointing the same way.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), lt ), act ), neg( trend( ratio( re, at ), 5 ) ) )
